title: The Great Gatsby
author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
setting: Long Island and Manhattan, in the summer of 1922, with Louisville and the Midwest behind them
lengthNote: Nine chapters and fewer than fifty thousand words — short enough to be read in an evening, and built to be
openingLine: In my younger and more vulnerable years my father gave me some advice that I’ve been turning over in my mind ever since.
summary: A bond salesman rents a cottage next to a mansion whose owner gives parties for strangers, and gradually works out that the parties are addressed to one woman across the bay. Fitzgerald releases the facts about Gatsby in the wrong order on purpose, so that a rumour becomes a host, then a lover, then a poor farm boy called James Gatz. The summer ends with two people dead, a third shot in a swimming pool, and a narrator who has decided that the people who survive are the ones with enough money to leave.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Great Gatsby
sourceText.note: References give the chapter. This transcription carries British spellings in places where the 1925 American first edition differs, and the quotations here follow it exactly.

atAGlance.label: Published
atAGlance.note: Charles Scribner's Sons, New York, with Francis Cugat's jacket painting.

atAGlance.label: Set in
atAGlance.note: Prohibition is three years old and the dates inside the novel fix the year precisely.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Gatsby's history arrives in Chapter 6, when four chapters of performance have already been established.

atAGlance.label: Earlier titles
atAGlance.note: Forms of the name of Petronius's party-giving freedman survived into the galleys Fitzgerald revised in Rome.

atAGlance.label: Reception
atAGlance.note: The reviews were mixed and the sales worse; the reputation the book now has was built after 1940.

structure.label: Chapter 1
structure.title: West Egg, East Egg and the green light
structure.summary: Nick Carraway introduces himself as a suspended judge, rents a small house in West Egg, and dines across the bay with his cousin Daisy and her husband Tom, who is reading about the decline of the white race and taking a telephone call from his mistress. On the way home he sees his neighbour on the lawn, reaching towards a green light.

scenes.title: The dinner at East Egg
scenes.summary: Daisy's voice, Jordan's boredom, Tom's theories, and a telephone that will not stop ringing.

structure.label: Chapter 2
structure.title: The valley of ashes
structure.summary: The road from Long Island to New York runs through a landscape made of the city's waste, watched over by a faded oculist's hoarding. Tom takes Nick to a garage there, collects Myrtle Wilson from her husband's business, and continues to a flat in Manhattan where the afternoon ends with a broken nose.

scenes.title: The apartment on 158th Street
scenes.summary: A party of six, a dog bought on the street, and Tom breaking Myrtle's nose for saying Daisy's name.

structure.label: Chapter 3
structure.title: Gatsby’s party
structure.summary: Nick is one of the few guests who has been invited. He hears three contradictory biographies of Gatsby before meeting him, finds a drunk in the library marvelling that the books are real, and leaves at the end of a night that closes with a car in a ditch and a driver who does not understand that wheels are involved.

scenes.title: Owl Eyes in the library
scenes.summary: A man in enormous spectacles establishes that the books have pages, which he treats as evidence of thoroughness.

structure.label: Chapter 4
structure.title: Gatsby’s story, Wolfshiem, and Jordan’s account
structure.summary: Driving into the city, Gatsby produces documents: a medal from Montenegro, a photograph from Oxford. Lunch introduces Meyer Wolfshiem, who fixed a World Series. Then Jordan tells Nick, in the Plaza's tea garden, the story of a white roadster in Louisville in 1917, and what the parties have actually been for.

scenes.title: Jordan's account
scenes.summary: Daisy in 1917, a letter the night before her wedding, and a request relayed from the man next door.

structure.label: Chapter 5
structure.title: Tea in the rain
structure.summary: Gatsby has Nick's lawn cut and fills his house with flowers for a meeting arranged four chapters and five years in advance. He knocks over a clock, recovers, and takes Daisy through the mansion, throwing shirts onto a table until she cries into them. The rain stops on cue. The green light becomes a light on a dock.

scenes.title: The shirts
scenes.summary: The house is exhibited as evidence; the tour ends with Daisy weeping over imported linen.

structure.label: Chapter 6
structure.title: James Gatz of North Dakota
structure.summary: The history the reader has been waiting for arrives at last: a boy who rowed out to a millionaire's yacht and changed his name at seventeen. Daisy comes to a party and does not enjoy it. Gatsby explains to Nick that Daisy must tell Tom she never loved him, and Nick suggests that the past cannot be repeated.

scenes.title: Dan Cody's yacht
scenes.summary: A name is invented on Lake Superior, and an inheritance of twenty-five thousand dollars is taken away by a lawyer.

structure.label: Chapter 7
structure.title: The Plaza, and Myrtle’s death
structure.summary: The parties stop and the servants are replaced. Five people drive to the Plaza in the heat and Gatsby asks Daisy to erase four years of her marriage; she cannot say the sentence. On the way back a yellow car kills Myrtle Wilson at the garage, and Nick learns who was driving. Gatsby stands in the shrubbery all night watching nothing.

scenes.title: The suite at the Plaza
scenes.summary: Tom takes the argument apart with the one fact Gatsby cannot dispose of: Daisy's past is her own.

scenes.title: The accident
scenes.summary: The exchanged cars make the wrong person responsible, which is how responsibility works in this book.

structure.label: Chapter 8
structure.title: Gatsby’s death
structure.summary: Nick hears the Louisville story from Gatsby himself, tells him he is worth the whole lot of them, and goes to work. Gatsby waits for a call, swims for the first time all summer, and is shot in the pool by George Wilson, who has spent the morning being pointed at the wrong car by the man who owned the right one.

scenes.title: The pool
scenes.summary: A gardener's plan to drain the pool is postponed by a day, and the day is the last one.

structure.label: Chapter 9
structure.title: The funeral, and Nick’s departure
structure.summary: Nobody comes. Wolfshiem sends regrets, Daisy and Tom have left no address, and the only mourners are Nick, Gatsby's father with a boyhood schedule written in the back of a book, and the drunk from the library. Nick breaks with Jordan, meets Tom on Fifth Avenue, and goes back to the Midwest.

scenes.title: The last page
scenes.summary: Nick lies on the beach at night and turns one man's backward-looking project into a history of the continent.

characters.name: Nick Carraway
characters.role: Narrator; a bond salesman from the Midwest
characters.summary: He opens by claiming a habit of suspended judgement and then spends nine chapters judging everyone he meets, often by their voices and their hands. The contradiction is the book's engine: reserving judgement is what gets him invited everywhere, and writing the account afterwards is where the verdict is finally delivered.
characters.clue: He rents the small house between two mansions, claims to be one of the few honest people he has ever known, and writes the whole thing down after going home.

relationships.label: neighbour, confidant and only mourner of

characters.name: Jay Gatsby
characters.role: Owner of the house next door; formerly James Gatz
characters.summary: A farm boy who invented a wealthy self at seventeen and then spent fifteen years assembling the evidence for him: a name, an accent, a war record, a mansion positioned directly across the water from one particular dock. His real crime is the belief that five years can be cancelled if you buy enough; the bootlegging matters less.
characters.clue: He throws parties he barely attends for guests he has not invited, and every one of them is aimed at a single house across the bay.
traits: formal to the point of strangeness

characters.name: Daisy Buchanan
characters.role: Tom's wife, Nick's cousin, and the object of the whole scheme
characters.summary: She is charming in a way the novel presents as an audible property of money, and she is not stupid — her remark about wanting her daughter to be a beautiful little fool is a report on what her intelligence has been worth to her. When the choice comes she does not make it, and she is not there when the bill arrives.
characters.clue: Her voice is the thing everyone remembers, she cries over a pile of shirts, and she lets someone else take the blame for a car.

relationships.label: loved by, and briefly in love with
kills, without knowing who she was

characters.name: Tom Buchanan
characters.role: A polo player with inherited money
characters.summary: Physically enormous, intellectually credulous, and secure in a way the novel puts down to his position, not his character. He conducts an affair openly, reads racial pseudo-science aloud at dinner, and wins the crucial argument by being the one person in the room whose past cannot be revised, without being right about anything.
characters.clue: He brought a string of polo ponies east, breaks a woman's nose over dinner, and tells a man with a gun which car to look for.

characters.name: Jordan Baker
characters.summary: A professional sportswoman who once moved a ball in a semi-final and left the rumour to die on its own. She is the novel's other unreliable narrator: it is her account in Chapter 4 that carries the history Nick cannot get from Gatsby, and she is careless in exactly the way Nick claims to despise.
characters.clue: She lies about a golf ball, drives badly on principle, and tells the story that explains the parties.

characters.name: Myrtle Wilson
characters.role: Wife of a garage proprietor in the valley of ashes
characters.summary: She has one room in Manhattan in which she is a different person, and the novel is precise about what her ambition can actually buy: a dog collar, some magazines, a tea set. She is the only character who dies because she believed a car was coming for her, and it was.
characters.clue: She keeps a small flat with a puppy in it, says a name she has been forbidden to say, and runs into the road at the wrong car.

characters.name: George Wilson
characters.role: Garage proprietor under the eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg
characters.summary: The only poor man in the novel, and the only one who acts on a moral conviction. He locks his wife in a room, mistakes an advertising hoarding for God, is given a name and an address by the man who has been sleeping with her, and does what he is pointed at.
characters.clue: He sells petrol beneath a pair of painted eyes, decides they belong to God, and is handed a description of a yellow car.

characters.name: Meyer Wolfshiem
characters.summary: Introduced as the man who fixed a World Series, and written with a stereotyping that a modern reader has to see and name. He is also the novel's clearest statement of how Gatsby's money was made, and the one associate who explains, in a letter, that he cannot afford to attend the funeral.
characters.clue: He wears cuff buttons made of human molars and made the reputation of a whole business, then sends his regrets in writing.

themes.name: The past
themes.summary: Gatsby wants more than Daisy’s love: he wants her to withdraw four years of her life from the record. The novel treats time the way it treats everything else in Gatsby's hands — as something he assumes money and effort can acquire — and the last page enlarges the same error into a national habit.
themes.development: Stated as a plan in Chapter 6, put to Daisy in the Plaza suite in Chapter 7, and turned into a history of the continent in the final paragraphs.

themes.name: Money
themes.summary: Fitzgerald presents class through sound and space, not numbers: a voice full of money, two eggs identical in shape and unlike in everything else, a valley between the houses and the city. Gatsby can buy the mansion, the shirts and the car, and the one thing he cannot buy is the sound of not having had to.
themes.development: Set up by the geography of Chapter 1, made explicit in Gatsby's remark about Daisy's voice in Chapter 7, and enforced by Tom in the same chapter.

themes.name: Self-invention
themes.summary: James Gatz becomes Jay Gatsby at seventeen on the shore of Lake Superior, and the novel calls it a Platonic conception — an idea of himself that he then has to furnish. Everything from the Oxford photograph to the word 'old sport' is evidence being assembled for a case nobody has formally brought.
themes.development: Withheld through four chapters of rumour, delivered in Chapter 6, and completed in Chapter 9 by a father with a boy's timetable written in the back of a book.

themes.name: Carelessness
themes.summary: The word runs from Jordan's driving in Chapter 3 to Nick's summary of the Buchanans in Chapter 9, and it is deliberately not the same as cruelty. Carelessness is what money makes possible: the ability to damage something and then to be somewhere else, with the address unavailable.
themes.development: Introduced as a joke about a badly parked car, and paid out when a woman is killed by one and nobody who was in it is inconvenienced.

themes.name: East Egg, West Egg and the valley of ashes
themes.summary: The novel's map does the sociology. East Egg holds inherited money, West Egg new money, Manhattan the places where the rules are suspended, and between them a valley where the city's ash is dumped and the people who shovel it live. Every fatal event in the book happens on the road through that valley.
themes.development: Laid out in Chapter 2, revisited on the way to the Plaza in Chapter 7, and the site of the accident on the way back.

themes.name: Nick’s judgement
themes.summary: Nick's opening claim to reserve judgement is worth testing sentence by sentence against what he actually does, which is to assign moral, social and aesthetic value continually. The novel is his account, written after he has left, and the reader's task is to notice whose interior life he grants and whose he does not.
themes.development: Claimed in Chapter 1, complicated by his silence about the accident in Chapter 7, and declared outright in Chapter 9 when he tells Tom what he thinks of him.

techniques.name: Retrospective first person
techniques.definition: A narrator telling, after the event, a story in which he took part.
techniques.inThisBook: Nick is writing from the Midwest the following autumn, which is why the judgements he claims to withhold are already in the prose: the verdict was reached before the first sentence was written.

techniques.name: Delayed disclosure
techniques.definition: Withholding the facts of a character's life until the reader has formed an impression without them.
techniques.inThisBook: Gatsby is a rumour in Chapter 3, a host in Chapter 4, a lover in Chapter 5, and only in Chapter 6 a poor boy from North Dakota — so the reader meets the invention before the man.

techniques.name: Symbolism
techniques.definition: An object whose meaning changes as a character's knowledge of it changes.
techniques.inThisBook: The green light is an unexplained gesture in Chapter 1, a dock light in Chapter 5 once Daisy is in the room, and a figure for the whole continent's appetite in Chapter 9.

techniques.name: Catalogue
techniques.definition: A list used for social observation, not description.
techniques.inThisBook: The guest list written on a railway timetable gives two pages of names and small disasters, and demonstrates without comment that nobody at the parties knows the host.

techniques.name: Weather
techniques.definition: Using heat, rain and light to time the emotional register of a scene.
techniques.inThisBook: Gatsby's reunion with Daisy is scheduled in rain that stops at the moment it should, and the Plaza confrontation is staged on the hottest day of the summer with a wedding band playing downstairs.

techniques.name: The ending
techniques.definition: Shifting at the end of a passage from reported speech and event into sustained rhythmic prose.
techniques.inThisBook: The last two pages leave the plot entirely for a meditation on Dutch sailors and the current, and the final sentence is built out of one subject, two participles and a metaphor that reverses the direction of travel.

quotations.text: “Whenever you feel like criticizing anyone,” he told me, “just remember that all the people in this world haven’t had the advantages that you’ve had.”
quotations.speaker: Nick's father
quotations.context: The advice Nick reports in the second sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The sentence sounds like generosity and is actually an instruction in class: it assumes both speaker and listener are on the advantaged side, and says nothing about what to do with that. Nick spends the novel among people who have had more advantages than he has, and never once applies the rule to them.

quotations.text: In consequence, I’m inclined to reserve all judgements, a habit that has opened up many curious natures to me and also made me the victim of not a few veteran bores.
quotations.context: Nick explaining the effect his father's advice has had on him.
quotations.analysis: The second half of the sentence gives the reason: suspending judgement is a technique for being told things. Within two pages he has called Tom's family enormously wealthy, Jordan incurably dishonest and the East a place he wanted in uniform, which is the contradiction the whole narration runs on — the reserve is a method, not a temperament.

quotations.text: it was an extraordinary gift for hope, a romantic readiness such as I have never found in any other person and which it is not likely I shall ever find again
quotations.context: The first description of Gatsby, given before the reader has met him.
quotations.analysis: The verdict is delivered in the opening pages, so the novel is not a mystery about whether Gatsby is admirable but an account of how Nick got there. 'Readiness' is the exact word: it names a capacity waiting for an object, which is what makes Daisy interchangeable with any sufficiently distant light.

quotations.text: ‘All right,’ I said, ‘I’m glad it’s a girl. And I hope she’ll be a fool⁠—that’s the best thing a girl can be in this world, a beautiful little fool.’
quotations.speaker: Daisy Buchanan
quotations.context: Daisy quoting what she said on waking from the ether after her daughter was born.
quotations.analysis: It is a quotation inside a quotation, which lets her disown it while saying it, and the setting matters: she is describing the hour in which her husband was elsewhere. The line is often read as cynicism about women, but it is a piece of career advice from someone who has calculated exactly what her own intelligence has been worth to her.

quotations.text: Involuntarily I glanced seaward⁠—and distinguished nothing except a single green light, minute and far away, that might have been the end of a dock.
quotations.context: Watching his neighbour stretch his arms towards the water at the end of the first chapter.
quotations.analysis: Three qualifications in one clause — nothing except, might have been — keep the light from meaning anything yet, which is precisely why it can later mean everything. Nick sees the gesture without the explanation, and the novel's method is set: the reader is given the reaching arms four chapters before the reason for them.

quotations.text: This is a valley of ashes⁠—a fantastic farm where ashes grow like wheat into ridges and hills and grotesque gardens; where ashes take the forms of houses and chimneys and rising smoke and, finally, with a transcendent effort, of ash-grey men, who move dimly and already crumbling through the powdery air.
quotations.context: The opening of the second chapter, describing the land between West Egg and New York.
quotations.analysis: The metaphor is agricultural — a farm, wheat, gardens — applied to industrial waste, so the valley is described as growing what the city throws away. The sentence takes four clauses to arrive at the men, and by the time it does they are made of the same material as the landscape, which is the book's flattest statement about who is disposable.

quotations.text: The eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg are blue and gigantic⁠—their retinas are one yard high. They look out of no face, but, instead, from a pair of enormous yellow spectacles which pass over a nonexistent nose.
quotations.context: The hoarding above the valley of ashes, left by an oculist who moved away.
quotations.analysis: The measurements are given in the present tense and in yards, as though the reader might go and check, and the eyes are explicitly attached to nothing — no face, no nose, no oculist. George Wilson will later decide they are God's, and the novel's care in establishing that they are an abandoned advertisement is what makes his mistake so exact.

quotations.text: I believe that on the first night I went to Gatsby’s house I was one of the few guests who had actually been invited. People were not invited⁠—they went there.
quotations.context: The opening of the first party scene.
quotations.analysis: The verb is repeated three times in two sentences so that invitation, the basic transaction of hospitality, can be shown to have collapsed. Nick's one small distinction — he was asked — is what qualifies him to narrate, and it also tells the reader that the parties are not for the people at them.

quotations.text: “I hope I never will,” she answered. “I hate careless people. That’s why I like you.”
quotations.speaker: Jordan Baker
quotations.context: Jordan, who has just nearly hit a workman's coat with her car, explaining why bad driving does not worry her.
quotations.analysis: She has explained that it takes two to make an accident, so her own carelessness is safe until she meets another one — and then says she hates careless people. The word she introduces here is the one Nick will use, six chapters later, to sum up Tom and Daisy; she hands him the term for the novel's central charge while demonstrating the offence.

quotations.text: “You’re a rotten driver,” I protested. “Either you ought to be more careful, or you oughtn’t to drive at all.”
quotations.speaker: Nick Carraway
quotations.context: In the car with Jordan, on the way back from a party.
quotations.analysis: Driving is the novel's practical test of character, and every collision in it involves someone who thought the other party would take care. The exchange also establishes the alternative Nick is offering the reader — be careful or get out — which is exactly the choice he takes himself at the end by going home.

quotations.text: “If it wasn’t for the mist we could see your home across the bay,” said Gatsby. “You always have a green light that burns all night at the end of your dock.”
quotations.speaker: Jay Gatsby
quotations.context: Showing Daisy the view from his own house, minutes after their reunion.
quotations.analysis: He tells her about the light in the flattest possible way, as a fact about her property, and ‘you always have’ gives away five years of watching. This is the moment the symbol is handed over to its owner, and the next paragraph records what it cost him.

quotations.text: Now it was again a green light on a dock. His count of enchanted objects had diminished by one.
quotations.context: Nick watching Gatsby immediately after he has pointed the light out to Daisy.
quotations.analysis: 'Count' is an accountant's word, and it suggests Gatsby keeps an inventory of enchantments the way he keeps one of shirts. The loss is caused by getting what he wanted: the light only worked at a distance, and the whole tragedy is compressed into the arithmetic of that second sentence.

quotations.text: There must have been moments even that afternoon when Daisy tumbled short of his dreams⁠—not through her own fault, but because of the colossal vitality of his illusion.
quotations.context: The end of the reunion chapter, as Nick leaves the two of them together.
quotations.analysis: The exoneration is explicit, ‘not through her own fault’, which makes it much harder to read the novel as a case against Daisy. ‘Vitality’ gives the illusion a life of its own, something that had grown, not something he held, and by this measure Gatsby’s tragedy lies less in losing her than in the fact that no actual person could have been what he had spent five years building.

quotations.text: The truth was that Jay Gatsby of West Egg, Long Island, sprang from his Platonic conception of himself. He was a son of God⁠—a phrase which, if it means anything, means just that⁠—and he must be about His Father’s business, the service of a vast, vulgar, and meretricious beauty.
quotations.context: The chapter that finally gives James Gatz's history, seventeen years old on the shore of Lake Superior.
quotations.analysis: Two incompatible vocabularies are welded together: Platonic philosophy and the Gospel of Luke, both used to explain a boy changing his name. The aside — if it means anything — is Nick refusing to guarantee his own sentence, and the last three adjectives make the object of worship squarely commercial without withdrawing the religious language.

quotations.text: “Can’t repeat the past?” he cried incredulously. “Why of course you can!”
quotations.speaker: Jay Gatsby
quotations.context: Answering Nick's suggestion that he should not ask so much of Daisy.
quotations.analysis: The adverb is the whole characterisation: he is not arguing, he is astonished that anyone would doubt it. Grammatically he treats the past as a direct object — something one performs again — and the rest of the novel is the demonstration that it is the one commodity his money cannot reach.

quotations.text: He wanted nothing less of Daisy than that she should go to Tom and say: “I never loved you.”
quotations.context: Nick explaining what Gatsby is actually asking for.
quotations.analysis: The demand is for a sentence, not an action, which tells the reader that Gatsby's project is editorial: he wants the record amended. When she cannot say the words in Chapter 7, it is accuracy that stops her, not cowardice, and the failure of one clause brings down the whole five-year scheme.

quotations.text: “Her voice is full of money,” he said suddenly.
quotations.speaker: Jay Gatsby
quotations.context: In Gatsby's house on the hottest afternoon of the summer, while Daisy is speaking in the next room.
quotations.analysis: Nick has spent two chapters failing to describe Daisy's voice and Gatsby settles it in five words, which is the one moment in the book where he sees more clearly than the narrator. It is also the diagnosis of his own defeat: what he loves in her is a sound produced by a security he was not born into and cannot purchase.

quotations.text: “They’re a rotten crowd,” I shouted across the lawn. “You’re worth the whole damn bunch put together.”
quotations.speaker: Nick Carraway
quotations.context: Leaving for work on the last morning of Gatsby's life, after a night of listening to the Louisville story.
quotations.analysis: Nick reports immediately afterwards that it was the only compliment he ever paid him, and that he disapproved of him from beginning to end — so the sentence is offered with the disapproval attached. The staging matters too: it is shouted across a lawn, at a distance, by a man on his way to the office, and it is the last thing Gatsby hears from anybody.

quotations.text: A new world, material without being real, where poor ghosts, breathing dreams like air, drifted fortuitously about
quotations.context: Nick's reconstruction of Gatsby's last hours, waiting beside a telephone that does not ring.
quotations.analysis: Everything solid in the novel is here declared unreal at the moment the illusion fails, and the ghosts are poor — the adjective does double duty for pity and for money. Nick admits he is guessing at all of this, so the most metaphysical passage in the book is explicitly an invention, made by a narrator about a man who invented himself.

quotations.text: “The poor son-of-a-bitch,” he said.
quotations.speaker: Owl Eyes
quotations.context: At the graveside, spoken by the drunk who admired the library in Chapter 3.
quotations.analysis: The only epitaph Gatsby gets comes from a man who went to one party and never met him, and it is four words of profanity. Set it against the two pages of lyric prose that close the book: the novel gives the plain human verdict first, and the grand one afterwards, and does not say which is truer.

quotations.text: They were careless people, Tom and Daisy⁠—they smashed up things and creatures and then retreated back into their money or their vast carelessness, or whatever it was that kept them together, and let other people clean up the mess they had made
quotations.context: After meeting Tom on Fifth Avenue and learning what he told George Wilson.
quotations.analysis: 'Things and creatures' declines to say people, which is how the sentence performs the carelessness it is describing. The judgement Nick promised on the first page to reserve is delivered here in the past tense, and the most damning phrase is the vaguest — 'or whatever it was' — because he has stopped trying to understand them.

quotations.text: gradually I became aware of the old island here that flowered once for Dutch sailors’ eyes⁠—a fresh, green breast of the new world
quotations.context: Lying on the beach at night before leaving the East for good.
quotations.analysis: The houses are made to melt away so that a seventeenth-century landscape can be laid over a twentieth-century one, and the colour green arrives from the dock light three hundred pages earlier. The move enlarges one man's obsession into a continental habit without ever quite saying that Gatsby stands for America.

quotations.text: Gatsby believed in the green light, the orgiastic future that year by year recedes before us.
quotations.context: The penultimate paragraph of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The verb ‘recedes’ does the work: the future is retreating, so pursuing it is already a backward motion. Nick has also switched to the first person plural here, which enrols the reader in Gatsby’s error two sentences before the famous image of the boats.

quotations.text: So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: Two participles pulling opposite ways — beating forward, borne backwards — leave the sentence with no net motion at all, which is the exact shape of Gatsby's five years. 'We' has replaced 'he' by now, and the last word of a book about the future is 'past'.

quotations.text: “I’m thirty,” I said. “I’m five years too old to lie to myself and call it honour.”
quotations.speaker: Nick Carraway
quotations.context: Ending the affair with Jordan Baker, who has accused him of throwing her over on the telephone.
quotations.analysis: He uses his birthday as a moral unit of measurement, as though self-deception had an age limit, and by his arithmetic the age for honourable self-deception ended at twenty-five. Jordan's reply — that she thought he was an honest, straightforward person — is the novel's last word on his opening claim.

timeline.label: F. Scott Fitzgerald born in Saint Paul, Minnesota
timeline.detail: Named for a distant relative who wrote the words of The Star-Spangled Banner.

timeline.label: Fitzgerald meets Zelda Sayre while stationed in Alabama
timeline.detail: The courtship, the refusal and the eventual acceptance after his first novel sold all feed the Louisville chapters.

timeline.label: The World Series is fixed
timeline.detail: The scandal that gives Meyer Wolfshiem his introduction in Chapter 4, and dates the world Gatsby's money comes from.

timeline.label: National prohibition takes effect, and This Side of Paradise is published
timeline.detail: The law that creates Gatsby's business and the book that made his author famous arrive in the same year.

timeline.label: The summer of 1922, in which the novel is set
timeline.detail: Fitzgerald was living at Great Neck on Long Island and beginning to plan a third novel.

timeline.label: The main draft is written in France
timeline.detail: A pencil manuscript of more than two hundred and fifty pages, then galleys revised so heavily in Rome that whole chapters changed shape.

timeline.label: The Great Gatsby is published on 10 April
timeline.detail: Charles Scribner's Sons, New York. The reviews were mixed and the sales well short of Fitzgerald's hopes.

timeline.label: Fitzgerald dies in Hollywood
timeline.detail: He was forty-four, at work on a novel about the film industry, and his reputation was at its lowest.

timeline.label: The Armed Services Editions distribute 155,000 copies
timeline.detail: A free paperback for service personnel put the novel into more hands in a year than it had reached in twenty.

timeline.label: Works published in 1925 enter the United States public domain
timeline.detail: The first-edition text became freely available for independent editions on 1 January.

places.name: Great Neck, New York
places.note: The peninsula of new money that Fitzgerald was living on, and the model for West Egg.

places.name: Sands Point, New York

criticalViews.position: The novel as a critique of the American dream
criticalViews.summary: The reading that took hold after the 1945 revival: Gatsby's rise and death are a verdict on a national promise that has become a demand for money and a woman, with the last page enlarging one man's case into a continental one.
criticalViews.counter: The novel does not equate Gatsby with America; Nick makes the connection himself, in prose he has already admitted is reconstruction.

criticalViews.position: The novel as a study of its narrator
criticalViews.summary: Attention shifts from Gatsby to Nick: what he omits, whom he grants an interior life, how much of the last two chapters he has invented, and what it means that he claims reserve while assigning value in every paragraph.
criticalViews.counter: Pressed hard, this can make the book a puzzle about reliability and lose the fact that Nick's judgements are mostly accurate.

criticalViews.position: The novel as social history of 1922
criticalViews.summary: A reading grounded in Prohibition economics, the motor car, the geography of new and inherited money on Long Island, and the racial anxieties Tom reads aloud at dinner in the first chapter.
criticalViews.counter: The novel is not a documentary; its dates and prices are exact, but its shape is closer to a fable than to a report.

criticalViews.position: The novel as a book about women who are not permitted to act
criticalViews.summary: Daisy, Jordan and Myrtle are given three different strategies — retreat into charm, professional coolness, and a rented room — and all three are punished or contained. The demand Gatsby makes of Daisy is that she revise her own history to suit his.
criticalViews.counter: The narration grants none of them much interiority, so the argument must be built from what Nick does not report.

essayQuestions.question: How reliable is Nick Carraway?
plan: Start with the opening claim to reserve judgement and set it against the judgements made in the same three pages.
Use Chapter 3 to show reserve working as a technique: it is what makes people talk to him.
Examine what he does not do after the accident in Chapter 7, and how little space the novel gives to that silence.
Look at Chapter 8, where he reconstructs a dying man's thoughts and admits he is guessing.
Conclude with Chapter 9: he delivers the verdict he promised to withhold, and the reader has to decide whether the account earns it.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the function of place in The Great Gatsby.
essayQuestions.focus: East Egg, West Egg, the valley of ashes and the Midwest
plan: Map the four settings and what kind of money each one holds.
Read Chapter 2 closely: the valley is between the houses and the city, so everyone must drive through it.
Note that every death in the novel happens on that road or in a swimming pool built with new money.
Use the Plaza in Chapter 7 as a neutral ground where the geography is temporarily suspended and the argument can be had.
Close on Nick's return to the Midwest, and on whether the novel treats it as a refuge or as a retreat.

essayQuestions.question: 'Gatsby's tragedy is that he got what he wanted.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Desire, distance and the green light
plan: Trace the green light through Chapters 1, 5 and 9 and note who is looking at it each time.
Use the count of enchanted objects in Chapter 5 to show possession working as subtraction.
Set against this Gatsby's actual demand in Chapter 6 — a sentence from Daisy, not a life with her.
Weigh Chapter 7, where Daisy's inability to say she never loved Tom defeats him before Myrtle dies.
Decide whether Chapter 8's unreal new world is Gatsby's discovery or Nick's invention.

essayQuestions.question: How does the novel present carelessness?
essayQuestions.focus: Money, consequence and who clears up
plan: Begin with Jordan's driving in Chapter 3 and her claim that it takes two to make an accident.
Follow the motif through the drunk in the ditch, the exchanged cars, and the wrong driver being blamed.
Note that the only people who cannot retreat are the Wilsons, and that both of them die.
Use Nick's verdict in Chapter 9 and examine its vocabulary — things and creatures, mess, whatever it was.
Ask whether Nick's own departure counts as an escape of the same kind.

discussionQuestions: Gatsby's history is withheld until Chapter 6. What would be lost if it came first?
Daisy is given almost no interior life by the narrator. Is that a limitation of the book or a statement by it?
The eyes of Doctor T. J. Eckleburg are an abandoned advertisement. Does it matter that George Wilson takes them for God?
Nobody comes to the funeral. What does the novel want the reader to conclude from a guest list of three?
Nick says he disapproved of Gatsby from beginning to end. Do the last two pages agree with him?
Tom tells George Wilson which car to look for. How much of the ending is an accident?

related.why: The other great retrospective narration by a young man remade by money he did not understand the source of.
Published the same year, and the other 1925 novel in which a single day exposes what a decade has cost.
An earlier American account of a woman who tries to act on her own account, and what the society around her does about it.
The same country seen from the other end of the economy, with a smash on a winter hill instead of a road accident.
Another study of a beautiful invented self maintained by spending, and of the people who pay for it.
